catalog_quote: The nominal system of Avokaya demonstrates three level tone patterns, High, Mid and Low. In addition, there is a Rising contour on short vowels, but no Falling contour on short vowels. Phonetically a Falling or Rising contour may occur on long vowels, but these long vowels are considered sequences of two Tone Bearing Units (TBU). ... In the nominal system, there are no restrictions on the occurrence of the three level tones, as shown by the representative examples below. (1) Monosyllabic nouns H ... M ... L ... (2) Disyllabic nouns HH ... HM ... HL ... MH ... MM ... ML ... LH ... LM ... LL ... In multisyllabic nouns a rising tone occurs only on the first syllable of disyllabic nouns with a monosyllabic root. [Kilpatrick 2004 OPSL 9 p. 88:] All Moru-Madi languages have three level tones, High, Mid and Low. Avokaya and Olubo have rising tones on short vowels as well as long vowels. ... Av…

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog holds Avokaya as tonal with an empty rule (Kilpatrick & Gilley 2004: three level tones H/M/L). Tucker's snippets say the same type (tone language, three level tones high/mid/low) and give no stress placement, so nothing to add or contradict; note Tucker's analysis rests mostly on Moru Miza with Avukaya forms cited comparatively.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tucker treats the Moru-Madi group (Moru Miza as the main exemplar, with Avukaya, Logo, Keliko, Lugbara and Madi compared) as tone languages with three level tones (high, mid, low) carrying lexical and morphological function; every scanned occurrence of 'stress'/'stressed'/'accent' in the volume was enumerated by earlier readers and re-checked here, and none states a word-stress placement or a stress property for Avukaya or for Moru-Madi generally (para 268's 'dynamic accent (stress) plays a greater role than tone' describes the Nilo-Hamitic languages by contrast; para 483 'In avukaya it is used mostly to stress the certainty of future happenings' is about a verbal particle).
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing stated (no stress statement at all for this group in the searchable scanned)
new_statements.exceptions: none; an incidental Lugbara remark on final -h 'especially on a stressed syllable with the vowel -a' is the only use of 'stressed syllable' and is not about Avukaya
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker's Moru-Madi analysis is 'represented mostly by Moru (Miza)' with Avukaya (his spelling), Logo, Keliko, Lugbara and Madi forms cited comparatively (e.g. 'ma Odzfliwa-i. I am an Avukaya'); Avukaya = Avokaya [avu], Sudan/DRC. The snippets come from the 1967 Dawsons reprint scan (archive.org easternsudanicla0001tuck).

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: both quoted passages are verbatim at the stated locators in the copies we hold (K&G 2004 pp. 235-236; Kilpatrick 2004 OPSL 9 p. 88). (2) The 'tonal' classification rests on a 2004 peer-reviewed phonology article by the long-term fieldworkers stating a three-level lexical tone system with free tone on nouns and tone classes on verbs; that is authoritative for tone and no listed or findable source disputes it. The weakness is only that 'no stress' is inferred from silence in a verb-tone paper and an orthography note; the two dedicated descriptive sketches (Callinan 1981, 10 pp; Dimmendaal 1986, 29 pp) are unheld and could contain an explicit stress/prominence remark that would refine the domain/the primary-stress rule fields, not the kind.
